title: Three flatbed trucks: Basie, Lunceford and the 767 band
summary: In 1939 Basie's, Lunceford's and the 767 band rode trucks in the Labor Day parade and traded blasts, which Lee says showed Los Angeles was not behind musically.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Marshall told me that in 1939, after having marched every year, they got flatbed trucks and Basie's band was in town and Lunceford's Luntzwood's band was in town and so they had 3 flatbed trucks ...
And it was Basie, Lunceford Luntzwood and the 767 band.
And that -- he said Basie's band had Killian Al Killion and Lunceford Luntzwood had Paul Webster, and he had his brother Ernie.
And each band had a high note trumpet player, and they were like ...

Oh yeah, like screaming all day, yeah. But I think the 3 of us were right together, though, and we'd take turns playing. When they would stop, then the next band would start, and they'd stop and the next would start. So, you know, we were like, us against the world, and so all these other bands, as I said before, were still playing all this march music, and so when we came along, you hear Basie on the truck, playing, and then you hear Luntzwood on the truck playing, and then you hear 767 on the truck playing -- and everybody is trying to get the other one, so ...

Those were highlights, really. Musically, Los Angeles was not far behind as people would have you imagine; they had a lot of good musicians out here and they did a lot of good things, because that Labor Day parade was a once a year thing, but it was a big event of the year.
